newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe inflation falls to seven-year low.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe inflation falls to seven-year low.

text.p: Zimbabwe's annual inflation fell to a seven-year low of 13.9 percent in November from 20.2 percent in October, surprising many local economic analysts who expected it to ease only slightly or remain around 20 percent.
Central Statistical Office figures showed inflation at its lowest since 1989.

Some economic analysts said the low figure was largely due to a fall in fresh food prices because of a bumper harvest, in contrast to November last year when Zimbabwe needed food imports to compensate for a crippling drought.
"I expected the decrease in inflation but what I didn't expect was such a sharp fall," said economic consultant John Robertson.
"But the decrease is mainly due to the fall in fruit and vegetable prices and there's been an important change in prices because of the good agricultural season we have had," he said.
But other economic analysts, including Anthony Hawkins of the University of Zimbabwe, were sceptical fruit and vegetable prices could have had such an impact on the inflation basket.

"It's a bit of a freak figure. I don't think one can read too much into this figure. The fact that the (central) Reserve Bank is tightening money supply indicates that the figure is not particularly meaningful," Hawkins said.
Two weeks ago, the Reserve Bank raised to 20 percent from 17.5 percent the statutory reserves banks are required to keep with it.

It said the measure was aimed at controlling money supply growth -- which has remained above the target of 22 percent per year fixed under economic reforms started in 1991. That growth threatens efforts to bring down inflation.
Money market analysts said they expected interest rates, which have been falling over the past six months, to creep up on the back of the Reserve Bank measure.
On Monday, one of the country's biggest commercial banks, Standard Chartered, raised its minimum lending rate to 29 percent from 28.5 percent, citing the hike in statutory reserves.
Other banks were expected to follow suit but Robertson said he would be surprised if they did so as he forecast interest rates to come down further as a result of the current inflation figure.
"Increasing the lending rate was the wrong thing to do and I think they (Standard Chartered Bank) will reverse that in a few weeks," he said.
